Fowler
FOW-ler
noun
From the Saxon fugelere, a bird-catcher, from fugel, a fowl. It renders the Hebrew yaqosh, one who lays snares — not an archer who shoots the bird openly but a trapper who takes it by concealment.

Biblical Definition

The fowler is the Bible’s picture of hidden danger, and every detail of his trade preaches. He does not hunt in the open; he sets a snare, conceals it, baits it, and waits, and the bird is taken without ever seeing what took it. So the psalmist’s comfort is aimed exactly where fear lives: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psa 91:3) — the two great terrors of the ancient world being the trap you cannot see and the plague you cannot fight, and God is named as deliverer from both. Solomon urges the same urgency upon a man who has become surety for his neighbour: “Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler” (Pro 6:5) — not negotiate, not delay, but tear yourself loose as a creature already in the hand. Most solemn is Hosea’s indictment, where the fowler is a minister of religion: “the prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God” (Hos 9:8). The man appointed as watchman to warn of traps has himself become the trap. And the great note of triumph belongs to the escaped: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psa 124:7) — the bird did not break the snare; the snare was broken.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who takes birds by snares, nets, or lime rather than in open pursuit; in Scripture the standing figure of concealed and patient danger.

FOWLER, n. A sportsman who pursues wild fowl, or takes them in nets or snares.

From the Saxon fugelere, from fugel, a fowl or bird.

The fowler’s art lies in concealment and patience rather than in open pursuit.

Rendering the Hebrew yaqosh, to lay a bait or snare.

Figuratively, one who lies in wait to entrap the unwary (Hos 9:8).

Key Scripture

Psa 91:3 — "Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence."

Pro 6:5 — "Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler."

Hos 9:8 — "The watchman of Ephraim was with my God: but the prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God."

Psa 124:7 — "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped."

Modern Corruption

Temptation is now imagined as an open contest a strong man may safely enter, when Scripture’s figure is a concealed snare which the bird never sees and from which the only wisdom is flight.

expand to see more

The corruption is the fantasy of the fair fight. Modern men, and modern Christians with them, tend to picture temptation as an opponent to be faced down — a matter of willpower, resolve, and accountability, in which a sufficiently determined man may stand his ground and win. Scripture’s dominant figure says otherwise. The fowler does not challenge the bird; he hides, baits, and waits, and the bird is in the net before it knows a net exists. That is why the Bible’s commands about temptation are so overwhelmingly commands to flee — flee fornication, flee idolatry, flee youthful lusts, flee these things, O man of God. Joseph’s victory was running out of the house without his coat, which looks like defeat and is the only recorded triumph in the chapter.

Recover the plain sense: the snare is concealed, therefore the wisdom is distance rather than valour. Pro 6:5 is a picture of undignified urgency — tear yourself away like a creature already in the hand — and the man who thinks such haste beneath him is the man the fowler is counting on. Add Hosea’s warning that a trap may wear the clothing of a prophet and stand in the house of God, so that the snare is not always in the obvious places. And rest the whole matter on Psa 124:7, which tells you who does the delivering: the snare is broken, and we are escaped. The bird has no power over the net. Its escape is always something done to the net, not by the bird.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon fugelere, a bird-catcher — the trapper who takes by concealment; Scripture’s figure of hidden temptation.

expand to see more

Fowler — Saxon fugelere, from fugel, a bird.

Hebrew yaqosh, to lay a snare or bait.

The trade depends on concealment, bait, and patience — never open pursuit.

Hos 9:8: the prophet himself becomes the fowler’s snare.

Psa 124:7: the snare is broken; the bird does not break it.

Usage

"The snare is hidden, so Scripture commands flight rather than confrontation."

"Pro 6:5 pictures undignified urgency — tear loose as a bird already in the hand."

"Psa 124:7 gives the deliverance to God: the snare was broken, not escaped by strength."
